'Surrendered his sword to the king' is incorrect because David had already taken Goliath's sword from Nob (wrong_detail).

content: At Nob, on what condition did the priest Ahimelech agree to give David the holy bread?
options: His servants must have kept themselves from women
David must offer a lamb as atonement
They must eat the bread right there in the sanctuary
David must leave his sword as a pledge
explanation: 1 Samuel 21:4–6 records that Ahimelech had only holy bread and required that 'the young men have kept themselves from women'; David confirmed they had done so, and the priest gave him the bread that had been removed from before the LORD. 'Offering a lamb as atonement' sounds ritually plausible but was not the condition stated (true_but_off). 'Eating the bread right there in the sanctuary' misrepresents the detail, since the condition concerned ritual purity, not the place of eating (wrong_detail). 'Leaving his sword as a pledge' reverses the reality: it was David himself who asked for Goliath's sword there (wrong_detail).

content: What kind of people gathered around David when he hid in the cave of Adullam?
options: Those who were in distress, in debt, and bitter in soul
The officers and mighty men of Israel
The priests who had fled from the city of Nob
The people of Keilah who came seeking help
explanation: 1 Samuel 22:2 records that 'everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul' gathered to David, about four hundred men. 'Officers and mighty men' describes David's army at a later stage, not at the outset in the cave (wrong_scope). 'Priests who fled from Nob' refers only to Abiathar, who arrived after the massacre recounted at the end of the chapter (wrong_scope). 'The people of Keilah' belongs to the story in chapter 23, outside this passage (wrong_scope).

content: How was Doeg the Edomite able to accuse the priest Ahimelech of helping David?
options: He was present at Nob when Ahimelech received David
He heard Jonathan recount it at the New Moon feast
He captured one of David's servants on the road
He was the gatekeeper of the shrine at Nob
explanation: 1 Samuel 21:7 records that Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen, was detained before the LORD at Nob; so in 22:9–10 he testified that he had seen Ahimelech inquire of God for David and give him provisions and the sword of Goliath. 'Hearing Jonathan recount it' is wrong because Jonathan had no involvement in the Nob incident (wrong_detail). 'Capturing David's servant on the road' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Being the gatekeeper of the shrine at Nob' assigns him the wrong role: he was Saul's chief herdsman (wrong_scope).

content: What ultimately convinced Jonathan that his father was truly determined to kill David?
options: Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan himself
Saul ordered David arrested in the middle of the feast
Saul sealed David's house during the night
Saul commanded his servants to hunt David down
explanation: 1 Samuel 20:33 records that Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to strike him, 'so Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.' 'Ordering David arrested at the feast' did not happen since David was absent (wrong_detail). 'Sealing David's house at night' belongs to chapter 19, when Michal helped David escape (near_passage). 'Commanding servants to hunt David' is also a scene from chapter 19, not a sign within chapter 20 (near_passage).

content: What was the sequence of who carried out the massacre of the priests at Nob?
options: The guards refused, so Doeg himself killed the priests and then destroyed the entire city
Doeg refused, so the guards had to kill the priests in his place
The guards killed the priests while Doeg killed only Ahimelech
Saul personally killed the priests and then commanded Doeg to burn the city
explanation: 1 Samuel 22:17 records that the king's servants refused to lift their hands to strike the priests of the LORD; verses 18–19 show that Saul then commanded Doeg, and Doeg himself killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod, then struck Nob the city of the priests with the edge of the sword, man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey, and sheep. The option reversing roles — 'Doeg refused, guards killed instead' — inverts the correct sequence of the text (wrong_detail, almost-right). The option 'guards killed, Doeg only killed Ahimelech' is wrong because it was Doeg who carried out the entire slaughter (wrong_detail, almost-right). 'Saul personally killed' is wrong about the subject: Saul gave the order but did not act himself (wrong_scope).

content: When they parted in the field, on what was the covenant Jonathan recalled grounded, and who wept more?
options: The LORD as witness between their two lines of descendants forever; David wept more
The LORD as witness between the two of them alone; Jonathan wept more
An oath of loyalty to Saul's throne; both wept equally
A covenant of brotherhood made before Saul; Jonathan wept more
explanation: 1 Samuel 20:41 records that they 'kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most'; verse 42 has Jonathan declare the covenant was sworn in the name of the LORD 'between you and me, and between your offspring and my offspring, forever.' The option 'witnessed between the two of them alone… Jonathan wept more' is wrong both in the covenant's scope (only between them rather than extending to their descendants) and in who wept more (wrong_detail, almost-right). The option 'oath of loyalty to Saul's throne' distorts the covenant's content, which is oriented toward David's house, not Saul's (wrong_detail, almost-right). The option 'brotherhood before Saul' is wrong about the setting: this scene took place privately in the field, away from Saul (wrong_scope).

content: When David heard that the Philistines were attacking and plundering the threshing floors, which city did he go to rescue?
options: Keilah
Hebron
Ziklag
Gath
explanation: David inquired of the LORD, then struck the Philistines and rescued the people of Keilah (1 Samuel 23:5). 'Hebron' is where David was later made king, unrelated to this event (wrong_scope). 'Ziklag' is the city Achish later gave to David, outside this passage (wrong_scope). 'Gath' is the homeland of the Philistines, not a city that was rescued (wrong_detail).

content: While David was hiding in the forest at Ziph, who came to find him to encourage him and strengthen his hand in God?
options: Jonathan son of Saul
The prophet Gad
The priest Abiathar
Abishai son of Zeruiah
explanation: Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David in the forest and helped him find strength in God (1 Samuel 23:16). 'The prophet Gad' had advised David on a previous occasion but not in this instance (near_passage). 'Abiathar' was the priest who had fled to David earlier but is not the one who encouraged him here (near_passage). 'Abishai' appears later in the narrative and does not belong to this passage (wrong_scope).

content: When Saul had nearly surrounded David on the mountain, what happened that caused Saul to break off the pursuit and turn back?
options: A messenger came to report that the Philistines had invaded the land
An earthquake split the mountain between the two sides
David sent men to negotiate peace with Saul
Jonathan intercepted his father along the way
explanation: A messenger came to tell Saul that the Philistines had invaded the land, so he stopped pursuing David and turned back to fight them; that place was called Sela-hammahlekoth (1 Samuel 23:27–28). 'An earthquake' is a fabricated detail — the text mentions only a mountain separating the two sides before the messenger arrived (wrong_detail). 'David negotiating peace' did not happen; he only evaded Saul (common_misconception). 'Jonathan intercepting Saul' is almost-right since Jonathan plays a role in the chapter, but he is not the reason Saul withdrew his forces (near_passage).

content: After secretly cutting off a corner of Saul's robe in the cave, why did David's heart strike him?
options: Because he had raised his hand against the LORD's anointed
Because he feared Saul would wake up and discover him
Because his men rebuked him for not killing Saul
Because he had damaged the king's precious garment
explanation: David's conscience smote him because he had stretched out his hand against the king, the LORD's anointed, and he said he would not harm him (1 Samuel 24:5–6). 'Fear of Saul waking up' is not the reason; the text speaks of David's conscience before God (wrong_detail). 'His men rebuking him for not killing' is the opposite of the text — they urged him to kill Saul rather than rebuking him (common_misconception). 'Damaging the garment' is almost-right since a corner of the robe was cut, but the real offense was against the LORD's anointed, not the robe itself (wrong_detail).
tags: David spares Saul in the cave

content: After hearing David's account and seeing the cut corner of his robe, what did Saul acknowledge about David?
options: That David would surely be king and the kingdom of Israel would be established in his hand
That David was more righteous than him but still had to remain in exile
That David was free to return to the palace as his son-in-law as before
That David would replace Jonathan as heir to the throne
explanation: Saul said, 'And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand' (1 Samuel 24:20). 'More righteous but must remain in exile' is only half right — Saul did acknowledge that David was more righteous than him (24:17), but he said nothing about exile (true_but_off). 'Returning to the palace as son-in-law' does not appear in Saul's words here (wrong_detail). 'Replacing Jonathan as heir' is a false inference; Saul only asked David not to cut off his descendants after him (common_misconception).

content: Chapter 25 opens with the death of which important figure, causing all Israel to gather and mourn?
options: The prophet Samuel
King Saul
The priest Eli
Jonathan son of Saul
explanation: Samuel died, and all Israel assembled and mourned for him; he was buried at his house in Ramah (1 Samuel 25:1). 'King Saul' dies later at the end of the book, not here (wrong_scope). 'The priest Eli' died early in the book (chapter 4), far outside this passage (wrong_scope). 'Jonathan' also dies at the end of the book alongside Saul (wrong_scope).

content: What was the name of Abigail's husband—a wealthy but harsh and wicked man who refused to help David?
options: Nabal
Nebal
Abanah
Nadab
explanation: Abigail's husband was named Nabal, a Calebite, wealthy but harsh and badly behaved (1 Samuel 25:3). 'Nebal' is a phonetic distractor that does not appear in the text (wrong_detail). 'Abanah' is a river near Damascus mentioned in the books of Kings, completely unrelated to this passage (wrong_scope). 'Nadab' was a son of Aaron—entirely outside this passage (wrong_scope).

content: When Abigail hurried out to meet David with provisions to avert disaster, what did she prepare?
options: Bread, wine, dressed sheep, roasted grain, raisin clusters, and fig cakes
Cattle, goats, honey, olive oil, and wheat
Silver, gold, garments, and weapons for the fighting men
Only two large skins of wine along with her own personal apology
explanation: Abigail took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred fig cakes (1 Samuel 25:18). 'Cattle, goats, honey...' names the wrong items from what the text actually lists (wrong_detail). 'Silver, gold, weapons' were not what she brought; she brought food provisions (common_misconception). 'Only two skins of wine' is almost correct since wine does appear on the list, but omits the large majority of the gifts (wrong_detail).

content: When did Abigail choose to tell Nabal about her meeting with David, and what was the consequence for Nabal?
options: She waited until morning when Nabal had sobered up, then told him; his heart died within him like a stone, and ten days later he died
She told him immediately in the middle of the feast that same night, and Nabal died of fright on the spot
She waited a full seven days before telling him, and Nabal flew into a rage and drove her away
She deliberately told him while he was still completely drunk so he would remember nothing, and God therefore forgave him
explanation: Abigail said nothing to Nabal while he was drunk; she waited until morning when he had sobered up and then told him everything. At that point his heart died within him and he became like a stone, and about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal and he died (1 Samuel 25:36–38). 'Died on the spot that same night' is wrong on both the timing and the sequence—she waited until morning and he died ten days later (wrong_detail). 'Seven days and then driven away' invents both the time interval and Nabal's reaction (wrong_detail). 'Told him while drunk so God would forgive him' reverses what the text says: Abigail explicitly waited until he was sober, and rather than being forgiven, Nabal was struck down by the LORD (common_misconception).

content: In her plea to David, what image did Abigail use to describe how the LORD guards David's life, in contrast to the lives of his enemies?
options: His life is bound in the bundle of the living with the LORD, while the lives of his enemies shall be hurled away as from the hollow of a sling
His life is like a tree planted by streams of water, while his enemies are like chaff that the wind drives away
His life is engraved on the palms of God's hands, while his enemies melt away like the morning dew
His life stands firm as Mount Zion, while his enemies collapse like a house built on sand
explanation: Abigail declared that David's life would be 'bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God,' while the lives of his enemies God would 'hurl away as from the hollow of a sling' (1 Samuel 25:29). 'A tree by streams of water / chaff' is imagery from Psalm 1, not from Abigail's speech (wrong_scope). 'Engraved on the palms of God's hands' comes from Isaiah 49, outside this passage entirely (wrong_scope). 'Firm as Mount Zion / house on sand' blends Psalm 125 and the Gospels—neither belongs to this text (wrong_scope).

content: Who came to tell Saul that David was hiding on the hill of Hakilah, leading to the pursuit described in chapter 26?
options: The Ziphites
The Keilites
The Amalekites
The Philistines
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 26:1, the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and reported that David was hiding on the hill of Hakilah. (A) is correct. (B) the Keilites were involved in chapter 23 but not here (wrong_scope). (C) the Amalekites were enemies David fought in another region (wrong_detail). (D) the Philistines were the foreigners among whom David would later take refuge, not the informers (wrong_detail).

content: On the night David crept into Saul's camp, who volunteered to go with him and descended all the way to where Saul was sleeping?
options: Abishai
Jonathan
Joab
Asahel
explanation: 1 Samuel 26:6–7 states that Abishai son of Zeruiah volunteered to go with David down to the camp at night. (A) is correct. (B) Jonathan was David's close friend but was Saul's son and did not take part in this mission (common_misconception). (C) Joab was Abishai's brother and a renowned commander, but he is not present in this scene (near_passage). (D) Asahel was also a brother of Abishai but is not mentioned in this passage (wrong_detail).

content: When David reached Saul's sleeping place without anyone in the camp noticing, what reason does the text give for why everyone slept so deeply and could not be roused?
options: A deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them
They were exhausted from a long day of marching
David had given the guards wine to drink
Abishai had struck down the sentries
explanation: 1 Samuel 26:12 records that no one saw, knew, or awoke because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them. (A) is correct. (B) exhaustion sounds plausible, but the text attributes the cause directly to God rather than fatigue (common_misconception). (C) there is no detail about giving the guards wine anywhere in this passage (wrong_detail). (D) Abishai wanted to kill Saul but David restrained him; there is no account of guards being struck down (wrong_detail).

content: When Abishai asked permission to strike down the sleeping Saul, David refused. On what principle regarding Saul's status did David base his refusal?
options: No one may put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless
Saul was David's father-in-law
The people would revolt if the king were killed
Killing a man in his sleep is an act of cowardice
explanation: In 1 Samuel 26:9–11 David says, 'Who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?' and leaves Saul's fate in God's hands. (A) is correct. (B) Saul was indeed David's father-in-law through Michal, which is true but is not the reason David states here (true_but_off). (C) fear of a popular uprising is never mentioned in the passage (wrong_detail). (D) the cowardice angle is a moral inference, not the reason Scripture records (common_misconception).

content: After leaving the camp, David stood on a distant hilltop and called out to rebuke Abner. What specific failure did that rebuke charge him with?
options: Failing to guard the king and therefore deserving death
Having fallen asleep during his own watch
Allowing David to escape from the surrounding forces
Having advised Saul to pursue David
explanation: In 1 Samuel 26:15–16 David rebukes Abner: 'You deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed,' using the spear and water jug taken from beside the king's head as proof. (A) is correct. (B) the text does not single out Abner as having fallen asleep — the whole camp slept because of the deep sleep God sent; the rebuke targets the failure to guard, not the personal act of dozing off (near_passage). (C) David was never encircled for Abner to let him 'escape'; David entered and withdrew on his own initiative (wrong_detail). (D) Abner is not identified anywhere as the one who counseled Saul to pursue David (wrong_detail).

content: To avoid being constantly pursued by Saul, David led his followers to seek refuge with which Philistine king at Gath?
options: Achish son of Maoch
Abimelech king of Gerar
Nahash king of Ammon
Hiram king of Tyre
explanation: 1 Samuel 27:2-3 tells us that David went over to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath, and stayed with him. (A) is correct. (B) Abimelech was king during the time of Abraham and Isaac, wrong era and wrong book (wrong_scope). (C) Nahash king of Ammon appears in chapter 11 and is unrelated here (wrong_scope). (D) Hiram king of Tyre belonged to the time when David was king and during Solomon's reign, not at this point (wrong_scope).

content: King Achish gave David a city to live in. According to the text, to whom did that city permanently belong afterward?
options: The kings of Judah
The kings of the Philistines
The tribe of Benjamin
The descendants of Achish
explanation: 1 Samuel 27:6 records that Achish gave Ziklag to David, 'therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.' (A) is correct. (B) the city was previously in Philistine territory, but once given to David it passed to the kings of Judah—reversing exactly what the text affirms (near_passage). (C) Benjamin was Saul's tribe and did not possess this city (wrong_detail). (D) the city belongs to the line of the kings of Judah, not to the descendants of Achish (wrong_detail).

content: While in Philistine territory, David raided the surrounding peoples, but why did he leave no one alive during his raids?
options: So no one could return to Gath and report what he was actually doing
Because the law of total destruction required killing all foreigners
Because Achish ordered that no prisoners be taken
To keep all the plunder for himself
explanation: 1 Samuel 27:11 says David left neither man nor woman alive to bring back to Gath, 'lest they should tell about us,' because he was deceiving Achish into thinking he was raiding Judah. (A) is correct. (B) the law of total destruction (herem) is a separate regulation and is not the reason the text gives here (true_but_off). (C) Achish gave no such order—David acted on his own to conceal his activities (wrong_detail). (D) the motivation was political and survival-driven concealment, not greed for plunder (common_misconception).

content: At the opening of chapter 28, the text recalls that Saul had previously done what with the mediums and spiritists in the land?
options: Had expelled them from the land
Had appointed them as royal advisors
Had imprisoned them in Gibeah
Had sent them to spy on the Philistine army
explanation: 1 Samuel 28:3 states that Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land. (A) is correct. (B) this is the complete opposite—he expelled them rather than employing them (common_misconception). (C) imprisoning them in Gibeah is a fabricated detail; the text says he expelled them from the land (wrong_detail). (D) sending them to spy is something that never appears in this passage (wrong_detail).

content: At En-dor, the figure of Samuel appeared and told Saul what would happen—far beyond what Saul had initially intended to ask?
options: Tomorrow Saul and his sons would be with him in the realm of the dead
The kingdom would be restored to Saul's descendants
David would die first in the coming battle
The Philistines would retreat without engaging in battle
explanation: 1 Samuel 28:19 records Samuel's words: 'Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me,' along with the LORD giving Israel into the hand of the Philistines; Saul had only wanted to know how to deal with the Philistine army but received the announcement of his own death. (A) is correct. (B) the opposite is true—the kingdom was torn from Saul's hand and given to David (28:17), requiring distinction from the false claim of restoration (near_passage). (C) it is Saul and his sons who will die, not David—the subjects are reversed (wrong_detail). (D) the text foretells defeat and battle, not a Philistine retreat (wrong_detail).

content: When the Philistines gathered their forces to fight against Israel, beside which spring did the Israelites encamp?
options: The spring of Gihon
The spring of Jezreel
The brook of Kidron
The spring of Adam
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 29:1, the Philistines assembled at Aphek, while Israel encamped by the spring in Jezreel. The spring of Gihon is associated with Jerusalem, not this battle (wrong_scope). The brook of Kidron is a stream near Jerusalem (wrong_scope). The spring of Adam has no connection to this context (wrong_detail).

content: Why were the Philistine commanders angry and demanded that Achish send David and his men away, refusing to allow them to go out to battle together?
options: They feared that mid-battle David would defect back to his former master Saul in order to regain favor with him
They suspected David had secretly offered sacrifices to the God of Israel
They felt that David's troops were too few to be of any use in the battle
They were angry because David had once killed their champion Goliath
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 29:4, the commanders feared that during the battle David would become an adversary to them, taking the heads of Philistine men to reconcile himself with Saul, his master. The offering of sacrifices is not mentioned anywhere; this is a fabricated detail (wrong_detail). The concern was not about the small size of his force; their worry was about his loyalty (wrong_detail). The killing of Goliath is indeed true and is referenced through the victory song in verse 5, but it was cited to illustrate the risk of betrayal, not as the primary reason for their anger (true_but_off).

content: When forced to send David away from the battle, how did King Achish evaluate David to his face?
options: As a treacherous rebel who was untrustworthy and suspect
As an angel of God, upright and good
As an idle servant who had merely lived off the land
As a priest set apart for a deity
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 29:9, Achish said to David: 'I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God.' Achish trusted David and did not regard him as a rebel; it was the commanders who were suspicious (wrong_detail). David was not viewed as an idle freeloader (wrong_detail). David was never described as a priest in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: When David and his men returned to Ziklag after three days, what did they find had happened to the city?
options: The Amalekites had raided it, burned the city, and taken the women and children captive
The Philistines had seized the city and established a garrison there
Saul had brought his army to besiege the city in order to capture David
An earthquake had leveled the houses in the city
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 30:1-2, the Amalekites had made a raid against the Negeb and against Ziklag, burned it with fire, and taken captive the women and all who were in it. It was not the Philistines (wrong_detail). Saul at this time was at the northern front fighting the Philistines, not besieging Ziklag (wrong_scope). There is no mention of an earthquake anywhere in the text (wrong_detail).

content: In the moment of crisis when the people spoke of stoning him, where did David find his strength?
options: He strengthened himself in the LORD his God
He was encouraged by the loyal pledges of his trusted warriors
He comforted himself by recalling his victory over Goliath
He asked King Achish to send reinforcements to rescue him
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 30:6, the people were bitter over the loss of their children and spoke of stoning him, 'but David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.' His warriors were themselves bitter at the time and were not a source of encouragement (wrong_detail). Recalling the victory over Goliath sounds plausible, but the text says no such thing; David relied on the Lord himself (common_misconception). David did not appeal to Achish for reinforcements; he inquired of the LORD (wrong_scope).

content: What did the Egyptian man that David's men found in the field do to help in the pursuit of the Amalekites?
options: He led David to where the raiding army was camped
He revealed the password to infiltrate the enemy camp
He showed the secret escape route the enemy had used to retreat
He provided a list of cities the Amalekites planned to attack next
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 30:15-16, the Egyptian (an abandoned servant of an Amalekite), after David swore not to kill him or hand him back to his master, led David down to where the army was spread out, eating and drinking and dancing. There is no detail about a password (wrong_detail). It was not a secret escape route but the location of the enemy camp (wrong_detail). He did not provide a list of cities about to be attacked (wrong_scope).

content: When some worthless men in the group wanted to refuse sharing the spoil with the 200 men who had stayed behind at the brook Besor because they were exhausted, what principle of distribution did David establish?
options: Those who went into battle and those who stayed with the baggage shall share alike
Only those who directly engaged in combat were entitled to the spoil
Each person's share was to be determined by the merit he had earned in battle
All the spoil was to be offered as a sacrifice to the LORD
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 30:24-25, David declared that 'the share of the one who goes down into the battle shall be the same as the share of the one who stays by the baggage,' and he made it a statute and rule for Israel to this day. The view that only those who fought should receive a share was precisely the position of the wicked men that David rejected (near_passage). Dividing by merit sounds reasonable but contradicts the equal-share principle David established (common_misconception). Offering all the spoil as a sacrifice is a fabricated detail; in fact, David also sent gifts to the elders of Judah (wrong_detail).

content: On Mount Gilboa, besides Saul himself, which members of his family also died in battle against the Philistines?
options: His three sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua
His three sons Jonathan, Ish-bosheth, and Abinadab
His two sons Jonathan and Amnon
His two sons-in-law Merab and Michal
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 31:2, the Philistines struck down Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. Ish-bosheth actually survived and later became king for a period, so this option is incorrect (wrong_detail). Amnon was a son of David, not Saul (wrong_scope). Merab and Michal were daughters of Saul, not sons-in-law, and they did not die in this battle (wrong_detail).

content: Why did Saul ask his armor-bearer to run him through with a sword, and why did he ultimately fall on his own sword?
options: Because he was critically wounded and feared falling into the hands of the Philistines to be mistreated
Because the LORD had commanded him to end his life there
Because he wanted to spare his children from being taken captive
Because his armor-bearer had betrayed him and forced him to take his own life
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 31:3-4, Saul was critically wounded by archers and said to his armor-bearer, 'Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me.' When the armor-bearer was too afraid to do it, Saul fell on his own sword. The LORD did not command this at all (common_misconception). The reason of protecting his children is fabricated; his sons had already died in battle before him (wrong_detail). The armor-bearer did not betray him — he was simply too afraid to strike the king (wrong_detail).

content: The fact that the men of Jabesh-gilead risked traveling all night to take down the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan reflects what about their prior relationship with Saul?
options: They were grateful because early in his reign, Saul had rescued their city from the Ammonites
They were following orders from David, who had sent them to attend to the burial of the dead
They did it to receive a reward from the Philistines for clearing away the bodies
They were direct blood relatives of Saul's household from Gilboa
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 31:11-13, when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, they retrieved the bodies, burned them, buried their bones under the tamarisk tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. This action arose from gratitude, because earlier (1 Samuel 11) Saul had rescued them from Nahash the Ammonite. David did not order this; he only learned of it afterward (wrong_detail). They acted out of loyal devotion, not to receive a reward from the Philistines — for it was the Philistines themselves who had hung the bodies to dishonor Saul (common_misconception). They were allied townspeople who remembered their debt of gratitude; the text does not identify them as direct blood relatives of Saul's household (wrong_detail).
